questions.text: Why can a linear-sweep listing agree with llvm-objdump yet still misrepresent the instructions that execute?

options.A: Both methods follow only direct branches and omit fallthrough paths.
options.B: Both methods require symbol sizes before decoding any instruction.
options.C: Both methods reject data bytes before attempting instruction decoding.
options.D: Both methods can decode embedded data as plausible instructions.

questions.explanation: Agreement checks the decoder against the same sweep strategy. Embedded data can decode successfully and shift instruction boundaries, so execution reachability needs separate analysis.

questions.text: Recursive descent stops at an unresolved indirect jump in grade at -O0. What evidence should you use to recover its case targets?

options.A: The table-base relocation, bounds check, and table-entry relocations.
options.B: The symbol names alone, assigning every function as a possible case.
options.C: The zero placeholder bytes alone, assigning every entry to address zero.
options.D: The linear listing order, connecting the jump to the next instruction.

questions.explanation: The base reference locates the table, the bounds check constrains its count, and the entry relocations yield targets while the object still contains placeholders.

questions.text: In recursive_descent, a branch appends instruction.target to worklist and sets address = instruction.end before continuing. Which path is decoded immediately?

options.A: The taken branch target, while fallthrough is discarded.
options.B: Neither path, because a branch terminates the whole traversal.
options.C: The fallthrough path, while the target remains queued.
options.D: Both paths in parallel, using one worker for each successor.

questions.explanation: The current inner loop continues from instruction.end. The target stays on the worklist for a later traversal, subject to visited-address checks.
